papers.title: Enabling Rapid Calibration of BCI Systems that Detect Movement-Related Cortical Potentials in Children with Cerebral Palsy.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interface neurofeedback (BCI-NFT) has shown promise for neuromotor rehabilitation, but its clinical adoption -- particularly in pediatric populations -- remains limited in part by the lengthy calibration required before each therapy session. This study developed and evaluated a deep-learning framework to reduce calibration requirements for movement-related cortical potential (MRCP)-based movement-intention detection in children with cerebral palsy (CP). Electroencephalography (EEG) was collected during repeated ankle dorsiflexion tasks across 27 sessions in four children with CP. A bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) network was evaluated using seven training strategies, ranging from conventional within-session calibration to cumulative cross-subject learning and transfer learning. Cross-subject cumulative learning achieved 91\% accuracy without within-session calibration, while the addition of transfer learning increased accuracy to 93\% with minimal within-session calibration. Both approaches significantly outperformed conventional calibration strategies and achieved the highest F1-scores and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) performance, demonstrating robust generalization across sessions and participants. These findings show that cumulative learning and transfer learning can substantially reduce calibration requirements while maintaining high decoding performance, supporting the development of clinically practical MRCP-based pediatric BCI systems.

papers.title: Bayesian nonparametric identification of spectrally distinct neural states
papers.abstract: Identifying neural oscillations is essential for linking fast brain dynamics to underlying cognitive processes. However, this is challenging because oscillatory events can be brief, embedded in 1/f-like background activity, and may comprise an unknown number of spectrally distinct states. Conventional approaches often apply narrowband band-pass filters to one or a few predefined frequency bands and then use amplitude thresholding to identify oscillatory events, but detection outcomes can be highly sensitive to these choices. Although recent unsupervised alternatives based on hidden Markov models (HMMs) address these limitations, they still require the number of states to be specified in advance and can underfit or overfit when this number is misspecified. We propose a Bayesian nonparametric method that identifies distinct oscillatory states while inferring an appropriate number of states directly from the data. This method combines time-delay embedding (TDE) with the Dirichlet-process Gaussian mixture model (DP-GMM). TDE augments the signal with time-shifted copies, enabling the DP-GMM to capture frequency-specific local autocovariance structures, while the Dirichlet-process prior adapts model complexity by pruning inactive components. We benchmarked the approach against a filter-based thresholding method and the time-delay embedded HMM using single-channel synthetic data designed to mimic neural time series (e.g., EEG, MEG, and local field potentials), with multiple frequency components masked by 1/f-like noise. In this setting, the proposed model reliably recovered multiple distinct frequency components under noisy conditions while also inferring the number of oscillatory states. Applied to a resting-state motor-cortex MEG dataset, the model identified multiple frequency-selective, short-lived oscillatory states alongside distinct aperiodic states with different spectral profiles. These states exhibited substantial inter-individual heterogeneity in peak frequency, occurrence rate, and power. Overall, this provides an unsupervised framework for discovering frequency-selective oscillatory states without predefining frequency bands or fixing the number of states.

ai.reason: Directly relevant unsupervised method for identifying spectrally distinct neural states with automatic model-order selection, transferable to EEG/sleep state analysis and interpretable feature extraction.
ai.summary: Proposes a Bayesian nonparametric method combining time-delay embedding with a Dirichlet-process Gaussian mixture model to identify spectrally distinct neural oscillatory states while inferring the number of states from data. Benchmarked on synthetic data and applied to resting-state MEG, the method reliably recovered multiple frequency components under 1/f-like noise and revealed multiple short-lived frequency-selective and aperiodic states with substantial inter-individual heterogeneity.

papers.title: Feature processing for single-trial semantic decoding from EEG: a factorial comparison with pre-registered replication
papers.abstract: Single-trial decoding of semantic processing from EEG is used in cognitive neuroscience, brain-computer interfaces and EEG-to-text research. Because single trials are noisy, the choice of features can determine how much information a decoder uses. Yet these fields use different features that have not been compared systematically: event-related potential studies decode the voltage time course (the waveform), EEG-to-text studies mostly the power of oscillations in frequency bands. We crossed four feature-processing choices--signal representation (waveform or band power), time window, normalization and channel set--into 640 configurations and decoded whether a stimulus fitted its semantic context in three tasks: visual word pairs, objects in visual scenes, and words in spoken sentences (40 participants per task). Eleven pre-specified comparisons were tested jointly. The signal representation had by far the largest effect on accuracy (mean generalized eta squared = 0.165, an order of magnitude above any other effect). Averaged over tasks and other choices, balanced accuracy was 56.6% with the waveform and 50.6% with theta-band power (chance, 50%), and adding band power to the waveform lowered accuracy by 1.8 percentage points, in every task. Both effects replicated, and were larger, in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants from three sites. Neither a finer time-frequency decomposition including the delta band (2-4 Hz) nor a different way of combining power with the waveform changed this conclusion, whereas the time window, normalization and channel set mattered little. For semantic decoding from single EEG trials, the waveform carries the information, and band power does not add to it.

ai.summary: A factorial comparison of 640 feature-processing configurations for single-trial EEG semantic decoding across three tasks showed that signal representation had the largest effect: waveform features achieved 56.6% balanced accuracy versus 50.6% for theta-band power, and adding band power to waveform reduced accuracy by 1.8 percentage points; these effects replicated and were larger in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants.

papers.title: High-Density EEG Signatures of Cataplexy in Narcolepsy Type 1.
papers.abstract: Cataplexy, the pathognomonic symptom of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), consists of sudden, emotion-triggered episodes of muscle atonia during wakefulness, with preserved consciousness. Although cataplexy shares features with REM sleep, its neurophysiological nature remains incompletely understood, particularly in humans. We investigated the electrophysiological signature of cataplexy using 128-channels EEG polysomnography in 10 drug-free NT1 adults. We analyzed 73 cataplexy epochs of ~30 seconds from 59 recorded episodes, compared with epochs of quiet wakefulness, N1 sleep, tonic and phasic REM, and direct-entry-REM-sleep. We compared hypnodensity profiles, computed with U-Sleep, of cataplexy and reference states. Regional and topographic spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands, absolute and relative to total power, were compared across states. EEG fingerprint robustness was assessed via within- and between-participant correlation distances. Cataplexy exhibited a distinct EEG profile with intermediate sleep-wake spectral features. Relative power showed scalp-wide reduced beta and increased delta-theta versus wakefulness, alongside elevated posterior beta and scalp-wide reduced theta-delta versus sleep. Absolute power showed increased global field power across most bands, supporting REM-like activity superimposed onto wake desynchronization. Hypnodensity analysis revealed a mixed-state signature combining wake-, REM-, and N1-like probabilities, supporting a hybrid state. Cataplexy differed from direct-entry-REM-sleep, arguing against a simple wake-to-REM transition. Variability analyses indicated greater between-participants than within-participant differences, suggesting partially conserved but individually expressed EEG signatures. Our findings support that cataplexy is a dissociated hybrid brain state reflecting co-activation of REM-like and wake-like synchronizations, constituting a unique pathological state with intermediate electrophysiological features.

ai.reason: Uses hypnodensity/sleep staging (U-Sleep), spectral power and normalization across states in sleep-wake EEG; strongly relevant to sleep staging and animal/human state classification methodology.
ai.summary: Used 128-channel EEG polysomnography in 10 drug-free adults with narcolepsy type 1 to characterize the electrophysiological signature of 73 cataplexy epochs versus wake, N1, and REM states. Cataplexy showed a distinct hybrid EEG profile with intermediate sleep-wake spectral features and mixed wake/REM/N1 hypnodensity probabilities, differing from direct-entry REM sleep.

papers.title: Integrating convolutional variational autoencoders and the Gaussian mixture model for efficient manifold learning and clustering of spatially preserved EEG topographic maps.
papers.abstract: EEG microstate analysis segments continuous brain activity into brief, quasi-stable topographic configurations whose quantity, duration, and transition dynamics index cognitive state and neuropsychiatric conditions. The standard algorithm, modified k-means (ModKMeans), operates in electrode space. It performs hard partitioning, assigning each data point to exactly one cluster, and provides no learned representation, no generative decoder, and no probabilistic soft assignment. In this research, a Convolutional Variational Deep Embedding model (Conv-VaDE) is designed, a topographic-map adaptation of Variational Deep Embedding (VaDE) that places a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) prior on the latent space of a convolutional variational autoencoder and jointly trains the encoder, decoder, and GMM. Microstate polarity invariance, the property that a topography [Formula: see text] and its sign-inverted counterpart [Formula: see text] index the same underlying configuration, is preserved through three coordinated mechanisms: sign-flip augmentation of the training set, a polarity-invariant reconstruction loss, and an encoder regulariser on the latent embedding. The model is evaluated on a sample of healthy participants ([Formula: see text] healthy adults, eyes-closed) from the LEMON resting-state EEG dataset using a multi-quadrant evaluation framework, with each method assessed in its native frame and cross-method comparisons performed via rank-based Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Conv-VaDE instead offers a focused set of capabilities the standard ModKMeans pipeline does not provide: a learned generative latent manifold (silhouette 0.232 at [Formula: see text], with very narrow cross-subject interquartile-range width [Formula: see text] across the 203 participants, indicating highly reproducible latent geometry), decoded GMM cluster centres inspectable as scalp topographies, probabilistic soft assignment for transitional states, and a generative framework supporting downstream representation analysis. A rank-based meta-criterion over silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, and Davies-Bouldin yields modal [Formula: see text] for Conv-VaDE (39.4%) and [Formula: see text] for ModKMeans (29.6%); [Formula: see text] is adopted to align with the canonical Lehmann A/B/C/D literature. Within the classical cluster-validity register, ModKMeans attains a higher silhouette and 4-5 percentage points higher Global Explained Variance at every K (Wilcoxon, BH-corrected, [Formula: see text]). The two methods occupy distinct positions in the methodological design space, with the cross-method comparison characterising the trade-off between direct electrode-space optimisation and learned generative representation rather than adjudicating method superiority.

papers.title: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation increases slow waves during human NREM sleep
papers.abstract: Slow waves are a hallmark of sleep homeostasis and a target for enhancing restorative sleep. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) can non-invasively deliver a low-frequency envelope to deep targets and has been shown to increase spectral slow-wave activity during sleep. It remains untested whether tTIS also alters discrete slow waves, how their cortical expression changes, and whether the field each brain receives relates to the response. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, 32 participants received 1 Hz tTIS and 11 a carrier-only control in 3-min episodes targeting the left insula/ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Combining high-density electroencephalography (EEG), source reconstruction and individualized field modeling, we found that tTIS increased slow-wave density by about 20% during and 30% after stimulation, across shallow and deep waves, with limited morphology change. The carrier-only control showed no detected density change. In source space, each wave involved more cortex in both arms, while wave origins did not change. A dose-response analysis showed that tTIS participants who received a stronger modeled field shifted further toward N3 sleep during stimulation, a relation not seen in the control. These results support tTIS as a candidate EEG-compatible tool for modulating slow waves and motivate individualized field modeling to interpret its effects.

papers.title: Cross-domain competition for memory reactivation resources during sleep
papers.abstract: Targeted Memory Reactivation (TMR) enhances the consolidation of both declarative and procedural memories. As previous research highlights the importance of cross-domain interactions in shaping memory consolidation, we investigated here whether interacting memories from different domains can be co-reactivated by TMR during post-learning sleep, and in turn enhance consolidation. In a fully within-subject design, twenty-four young, healthy participants learned both a motor and an object sequence learning task that were linked or not by a shared ordinal structure. TMR cues associated only with the object task were presented during post-learning non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep which was monitored with electroencephalography (EEG) during a 90-minute nap. We tested whether reactivating object memories would indirectly reactivate the linked motor memory. Behavioral results showed no overall effect of association but indicated that TMR disrupted object memory consolidation without indirectly affecting performance on the linked motor task. Sleep EEG data point to a competition for reactivation resources whereby slow oscillation (SO; 0.5-2 Hz) and spindle activity (12-16 Hz) involved in both memory protection and potentiation during sleep were preferentially allocated to the covert consolidation of the motor trace at the expense of object memory. These findings suggest that cross-domain memories sharing a common learning structure compete for consolidation resources during post-learning sleep.

ai.reason: NREM sleep EEG with slow-oscillation/spindle analysis relevant to sleep-state and spectral methods, though memory-themed.
ai.summary: In a within-subject nap study with 24 participants, targeted memory reactivation cues for an object sequence task disrupted object memory consolidation without indirectly improving a linked motor task, and sleep EEG indicated that slow oscillation and spindle activity were preferentially allocated to the motor trace, suggesting cross-domain competition for reactivation resources.

papers.title: Characterizing the heterogeneity of Alzheimer's disease through EEG normative modeling.
papers.abstract: To integrate normative modeling with non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) to characterize individualized brain functional abnormalities across Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI), thereby elucidating disease heterogeneity and enabling biologically informed stratification. We constructed sex-specific normative age models for the small-world (SW) architecture of hemispheric EEG networks and quantified individual SW deviations in 160 AD, 161 MCI, and 769 healthy controls (HCs) across multiple datasets. Individual deviation profiles were used to delineate sex-dependent topological alterations across the cognitive spectrum. We further performed unsupervised clustering to identify subtypes for both AD and MCI, and characterized their inter-subtype similarities and differences. The identified subtypes were rigorously validated for internal/external consistency and specificity. EEG normative models (NMs) captured frequency-specific aging trajectories of SW organization and revealed progressive sex-related divergence in SW deviation with cognitive decline. Both MCI and AD cohorts were consistently classified into two EEG-defined subtypes with distinct intrinsic dysconnectivity patterns and cognitive profiles, despite no differences in canonical multimodal MRI measures. Subtype-1 exhibited relatively preserved network organization and distinctive neurocognitive recovery patterns, whereas subtype-2 showed widespread network disruption and poorer clinical outcomes. Cross-stage analyses demonstrated shared EEG signatures between corresponding MCI and AD subtype pairs, supporting their biological continuity. Multidimensional validation confirmed the robustness and generalizability of our subtyping framework. NM-guided EEG profiling reveals clinically meaningful neurobiological heterogeneity cross the AD spectrum and identifies a high-risk MCI subtype before detectable cerebral atrophy. This framework provides an individualized, non-invasive strategy for early AD subtyping and prognostic stratification.

papers.title: Automated action potential parameter analysis for reproducible electrophysiological measurements in neurons.
papers.abstract: Quantitative analysis of action potential (AP) waveforms is central to studies of neuronal excitability, ion channel function, disease mechanisms and pharmacological modulation. However, AP analysis is still often performed using partially manual workflows or proprietary software environments that can constrain the amount of information extracted from APs and limit reproducibility, transparency and throughput. Here, we present a freely available, open-source software tool for extracting AP parameters, developed for use with the OriginLab software package Origin/OriginPro. APpar detects APs from membrane voltage recordings using a user-defined derivative criterion and calculates a comprehensive set of excitability parameters, including resting membrane potential, voltage threshold, overshoot, afterhyperpolarization (AHP), AP amplitude, rise and decay time, AP duration, AP half-width, AP width at 0 mV, AP area above voltage threshold, dV/dtmax, dV/dtmin and interspike interval for the respective AP. Because AP threshold is a particularly sensitive and method-dependent measurement, APpar includes a TRUE-threshold validation algorithm. After the initial forward dV/dt threshold crossing is identified, the software finds AP overshoot, searches backward to the closest preceding local dV/dt maximum, then searches backward to the user-defined dV/dt crossing and recalculates AP parameters from this validated threshold point. We validated APpar using APs from dorsal root ganglion neuron current-clamp recordings, including copied identical APs, current-evoked repetitive firing and long-duration spontaneous firing. The software produced stable measurements from identical copied APs and extracted dynamic changes in AP parameters across repetitive and spontaneous firing sequences. APpar provides a transparent, customizable and Origin-compatible framework for reproducible AP analysis in neuronal electrophysiology. KEY POINTS: Action potential (AP) waveforms contain important information about neuronal excitability and function of the underlying ion channels, but their analysis is often performed using partially manual, labour-intensive workflows, constraining the amount of information extracted from each AP, which can limit reproducibility and throughput. Measurements such as AP threshold, amplitude and duration depend strongly on how threshold is defined, creating variability between studies and laboratories. We developed APpar, a freely available open-source software tool that automatically detects APs and extracts a comprehensive set of waveform and excitability parameters within the widely used Origin/OriginPro environment. APpar incorporates a novel TRUE-threshold (Temporally Reversed Unsupervised Extraction of the Threshold) validation algorithm that improves the consistency of derivative-based threshold detection while preserving user control over physiologically meaningful analysis settings. Validation using dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neuron recordings showed that APpar provides stable measurements and enables efficient analysis of single AP, repetitive and spontaneous firing, supporting reproducible studies of neuronal excitability and ion channel function.

papers.title: A Neuro-Inspired Dual-Pathway Attention Network for EEG-Based Identity Recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals have shown promise for biometric recognition due to their intrinsic liveness detection. However, their practical deployment remains limited. The main obstacles are non-stationary drift, scarce labeled data, and fluctuating signal quality. Most existing models adopt static computation graphs, which are ill-equipped to handle these variations. We propose a dual-pathway architecture that separates a data-driven bottom-up perceptual extractor from a prior-guided top-down modulator. A quality-aware gate computes instantaneous signal stability from channel-wise and temporal variances. It dynamically fuses the two pathways: bottom-up features dominate when the signal is clean, and identity priors take over when noise is high. Deep residual connections and pyramid fusion stabilize multi-scale learning. On the DEAP dataset, our method achieves 93.8% accuracy, which is 5.3 percentage points higher than the best baseline. On THU-EP, it reaches 97.2%. In cross-session tests on the noisy SEED-IV dataset, performance drops only 2.5% in Session 2 and 5.2% in Session 3. With only 1% of the training data on THU-EP, the model still attains 76.8% accuracy. Dynamic, signal-dependent fusion improves accuracy, cross-session robustness, and data efficiency. This work offers a practical, low-enrollment solution for patient identity verification, electronic health record access, and brain-computer interface authentication in clinical and mobile settings. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cangtianhaoxue/ DPRAN.git.

papers.title: EEG biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases: Machine learning applications and clinical trial insights.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are diverse conditions characterised by selective dysfunction and progressive loss of neurons, glial cells, and neural networks in the brain and spinal cord. NDs pose a major global health challenge due to ageing populations and lack of cure, prompting interest in developing algorithms for early detection and biomarkers. Electroencephalography (EEG), a non-invasive and cost-effective tool, has emerged as a promising method for identifying neural signatures of NDs. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) have further enabled automated diagnosis, disease monitoring, and prognostic modelling using EEG data. This review synthesises evidence from 226 studies, mapping the current landscape of EEG-based diagnosis, prognosis, and patient stratification across various NDs. Unlike prior reviews, it provides a comprehensive overview across multiple disorders, including rare ones, and evaluates the role of ML and AI in clinical translation. We analyse research trends, EEG acquisition and preprocessing, and the development of biomarkers for disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment monitoring, and patient stratification. Spectral power, event-related potentials, and connectivity are the main features, with support vector machines and neural networks as the primary classifiers. We review clinical trials involving EEG in NDs and highlight open-source EEG repositories to support reproducibility and data sharing. Despite promising results, challenges such as small sample sizes, methodological differences, limited model interpretability, and gaps in clinical validation remain. The review highlights the potential of EEG combined with ML/AI for early diagnosis and therapy, while outlining future directions through standardised pipelines, explainable models, and collaborative open data initiatives.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled quality assurance for point-of-care electroencephalographic cap placement by inexperienced users.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) remains inaccessible in many health care settings, including low- and middle-income countries and point-of-care environments where trained EEG technologists are unavailable. Although low-cost EEG systems enable inexperienced users to acquire EEG, reliable acquisition also requires quality assurance of accurate electrode array positioning. We developed an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled tool to address this need. We conducted a prospective randomized crossover validation study comparing AI-guided EEG cap fitting by inexperienced users with placement by an expert EEG technologist. A blinded expert quantified positioning error against International 10-20 System targets and independently rated overall placement as optimal, usable, or incorrect. Thirty participants completed 60 placement trials. Mean absolute positioning error was .938 cm with app-guided and .855 cm with expert placement. The mean paired difference was .084 cm (90% confidence interval = .024-.143), demonstrating noninferiority against the prespecified .5-cm margin. Clinically acceptable placement (optimal or usable) was achieved in 28 of 30 (93.3%) app-guided and 30 of 30 (100%) expert trials. AI-enabled quality assurance enabled inexperienced users to achieve electrode array positioning noninferior to expert placement, supporting its potential use in expanding access to point-of-care EEG.

ai.summary: In a prospective randomized crossover validation study with 30 participants and 60 placement trials, the authors developed and tested an AI-enabled tool for quality assurance of EEG cap placement by inexperienced users compared with expert technologist placement. Mean absolute positioning error was 0.938 cm with app guidance versus 0.855 cm with expert placement, demonstrating noninferiority against a prespecified 0.5-cm margin, with clinically acceptable placement achieved in 93.3% of app-guided versus 100% of expert trials.

papers.title: Treadmill Walking Differentially Modulates Early Auditory Responses to Standard and Deviant Sounds.
papers.abstract: People often encounter environmental sounds while walking without attending to them, but it is unclear whether walking alters early cortical responses to these sounds. We recorded 32-channel electroencephalography from 22 healthy young adults during a passive auditory frequency-oddball paradigm. Conditions were sitting and treadmill walking without an object, with a water-filled cup or with a clay-filled cup matched for mass and apparent fill height. The four conditions were compared in two pairs: sitting versus walking without carrying, and water versus clay carrying. In each comparison, we examined standard- and deviant-evoked responses in the N1 window and amplitude in the mismatch-negativity window. The sitting versus walking-without-carrying comparison showed a significant stimulus-type by movement-condition interaction 80-130 ms after sound onset. In separate, unadjusted comparisons of sitting and walking for each stimulus type, the deviant-evoked response was attenuated during walking, whereas the standard-evoked response did not differ significantly between conditions. Sensitivity analyses in the same participants yielded a smaller interaction estimate with the lowest high-pass cutoff, but filter-setting differences were unclear. In the comparison of water and clay carrying, the conditions differed kinematically, but no additional modulation of the measured auditory responses was detected. The comparison of sitting and treadmill walking showed that walking-related changes in early auditory responses differed between standard and deviant sounds. However, the contributions of frequency, probability and adaptation to this response difference could not be separated.

papers.title: Frontoparietal Hyperconnectivity as a Single-Subject Neural Signature of Chronic Tinnitus
papers.abstract: Chronic tinnitus, the persistent perception of phantom sound, affects 14 to 15\% of adults yet lacks a validated neurophysiological biomarker, in part because group-average EEG analyses obscure the individual heterogeneity that defines the condition. In a multi-site case-control study of 544 participants (268 with tinnitus, mean age 45.4 {+/-} 16.1 years, 52\% female) across seven independent international sites, we applied normative modelling to quantify how far each person's resting-state EEG deviates from age- and hearing-adjusted healthy norms. Fusing spectral-power and connectivity deviations, a classifier detected tinnitus with an area under the curve of 0.832 under site-grouped cross-validation of precomputed normative features. The single most discriminative feature, rank-stable across all seven sites, was theta-band right orbitofrontal (pars orbitalis) connectivity, which dominated attribution by roughly an order of magnitude. Theta hyperconnectivity spanned frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks while primary auditory cortex showed negligible involvement, favouring failed top-down gating over bottom-up auditory overactivity. Features identifying tinnitus presence were orthogonal to symptom severity. These findings reframe chronic tinnitus as a frontoparietal attention-network disorder and nominate right orbitofrontal theta hyperconnectivity as a site-robust diagnostic feature. Data were collected within the TIDE project (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06520865).

papers.title: EEG Source Localization with High-Resolution 40-Tissue Head Models: A Comparative Study with MEG during Photic Driving
papers.abstract: While MEG source localization pipelines often employ head models of one single compartment with homogeneous conductivity, researchers and clinicians use at least 3 different layers in head models for EEG source localization. Recent AI-based segmentation makes it possible to generate individualized head models with 40 high-resolution, non-nested tissues. We present a pipeline that can make use of, and test, these highly realistic models for EEG source localization: with the boundary element fast multipole method (BEM-FMM), we compute transcranial electric stimulation (TES) solutions on the full 40-tissue geometry and use them reciprocally to obtain the EEG leadfields. Out approach runs on a single modest workstation, requiring approximately 4.5 min per EEG channel for a mesh of about one million elements at a relative residual of 1e-4. We applied the pipeline to six participants undergoing intermittent photic stimulation at half their individual alpha peak frequency, comparing 61-channel EEG source localizations from 40-tissue and 5-layer models with each other and with localizations from simultaneously recorded MEG. We further compared noiseless synthetic EEG topographies of the two models across the entire cortex. The two models produced highly consistent EEG source localizations (weighed relative difference below 3%), both in close agreement with the MEG localizations within the visual cortex. The synthetic topographies also agreed closely, with differences scaling approximately linearly with the angle between the source orientations of the two models, underscoring the importance of accurate source normals in fixed-orientation source models. These results establish 40-tissue models as a practical and robust basis for EEG source localization, and open the way to applications where nested geometries cannot represent the anatomy, such as infants or patients with skull defects, injuries, or tumors.

ai.reason: High-resolution forward modeling pipeline is useful neuroimaging methodology but tangential to time-series classification and sleep applications.
ai.summary: The authors present a pipeline using the boundary element fast multipole method to compute EEG leadfields on high-resolution 40-tissue head models and applied it to six participants during photic driving, comparing 61-channel EEG source localizations from 40-tissue and 5-layer models with each other and with simultaneously recorded MEG. The two models produced highly consistent EEG source localizations (weighted relative difference below 3%), both in close agreement with MEG localizations within the visual cortex, establishing 40-tissue models as a practical and robust basis for EEG source localization.

papers.title: Childhood emotional neglect modulates emotional face processing in healthy young adults: An ERP study.
papers.abstract: Childhood Emotional Abuse (EA) and Emotional Neglect (EN) have been proposed to have long-term effects on emotion processing and their neurophysiological correlates in a wide range of clinical populations, yet evidence from non-clinical samples remains limited. The aim of this study is to examine associations between childhood EA and EN and early perceptual (P100, N170) and later evaluative (late positive potential, LPP) stages of emotional face processing in healthy young adults. Fifty-four participants (15 M) (Mean age: 23.9; SD: 3.83) from the Puglia region (Italy) completed a facial emotion categorization task while their neurophysiological activity was recorded through a 32-channel EEG. Childhood EA and EN were retrospectively assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ). Event-related potential (ERP) peaks, latencies and amplitudes were analyzed using repeated-measures linear mixed-effects models with EA and EN as continuous predictors. EN, but not EA, was associated with increased P100 amplitude across facial expressions [F(1,54) = 7.46, p = .008, ηp2 = 0.121] and shorter N170 latency [F(1,54) = 4.27, p = .044, ηp2 = 0.073]. For the LPP, a significant EN × Emotional Valence interaction emerged [F(2,108) = 3.68, p = .029, ηp2 = 0.064], with a stronger negative association between EN and LPP amplitude for happy than for angry faces; Behaviourally, an EN × Emotional Valence interaction emerged for reaction time [F(2,5954.2) = 4.12, p = .016, ηp2 = 0.001], with slower responses to neutral faces at higher EN and for accuracy. Also, a Valence interaction with both EN [χ2(2) = 13.99, p < .001] and EA [χ2(2) = 17.71, p < .001] emerged. More in detail, the more the EN is, the higher accuracy for happy faces is, while the more EA is, the higher accuracy for angry faces is. Overall, EN was associated with variation across both early and late stages of emotional face processing, whereas EA showed no detectable ERP associations. At the behavioral level, both EN and EA showed valence-specific associations with accuracy (higher accuracy for happy and angry faces, respectively), and EN was additionally associated with slower responses to neutral faces. These preliminary findings suggest that, even in a non-clinical sample, childhood EN is more closely associated with the temporal dynamics of emotional face processing than EA.

papers.title: Preparatory beta activity reflects the precision demands of an upcoming movement
papers.abstract: Noise and external disturbances continuously push the limb away from its intended path, but not every deviation compromises the goal of an action. The accuracy constraints of a task define the range of acceptable endpoints and thereby set its precision demands, that is, how much noise must be attenuated for the task to succeed. Whether neural activity during movement preparation reflects these precision demands remains largely unexplored. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while healthy human participants (n = 27) prepared reaching movements toward narrow or wide targets at the same location and with the same timing constraints. An instructed delay before the go cue allowed preparatory activity to be isolated, and mechanical perturbations were applied during movement to probe feedback responses. Narrow targets led to more precise movements, with greater endpoint accuracy, lower variability and smaller perturbation-induced deviations. This was achieved without a reduction in movement speed, and involved greater muscle co-activation and larger long-latency responses to perturbations. Before movement onset, beta power (13-30 Hz) was lower for narrow than for wide targets, an effect that emerged late in the delay period and was concentrated over bilateral parieto-occipital electrodes. In contrast, alpha (8-12 Hz) and theta (4-7 Hz) activity did not differ between conditions. These findings demonstrate that preparatory beta activity is sensitive not only to kinematic requirements of the movement but also the precision with which it must be produced.

papers.title: How Perceived Traits Modulate the Neural Processing of Reward During Reinforcement Learning.
papers.abstract: Humans infer others' traits through positive and negative feedback, and these perceived traits, in turn, shape how individuals perceive others' behavior. Although previous studies have investigated the neural basis of reward and trait learning, the temporal dynamics by which trait-level learning signals modulate reward-related brain responses during learning remain poorly understood. In this study, we used reinforcement learning models to separate participants' processing of reward and generosity prediction errors (PEs), and used EEG to examine how perceived traits modulate the neural processing of reward. Behavioral analyses indicated that both reward and perceived generosity influenced decision making during the learning phase. In the test phase, perceived trait information played a more significant role in guiding decisions. Neurally, positive reward PEs elicited larger reward positivity amplitudes, stronger delta power, and reduced N400 amplitudes compared to negative reward PEs only when generosity PEs were negative. This pattern may reflect an increased focus on reward outcomes when experienced generosity is less than expected during the learning phase. These results elucidate how trait learning asymmetrically modulates reward salience and evaluation, a mechanism that may promote the prioritization of social knowledge in future choices.

papers.title: Late cortical dynamics mediate numerosity illusions induced by symmetry.
papers.abstract: Numerosity perception enables us to quickly estimate the number of objects in a visual scene, a fundamental skill supporting efficient interaction with the environment. In this study, we tracked how the human brain transforms physical inputs into numerical percepts. Using EEG, we characterized the temporal dynamics of how numerosity-related signals are integrated with spatial configuration cues that shape perception. We leveraged on a visual illusion in which dot arrays appear less numerous when arranged symmetrically rather than randomly. Participants viewed dot arrays of varying physical or perceived numerosity, illusorily altered by the dots' spatial arrangement. Both univariate and multivariate analyses revealed that physical numerosity was decodable from occipitoparietal electrodes as early as ~50 ms after stimulus onset, independently of low-level features such as convex hull, density, individual and total item area. Spatial arrangement was represented later, from ~150 ms, and perceived numerosity, biased by symmetry-induced grouping, emerged at a similar latency. These results indicate that early neural signals encode physical numerosity directly, whereas the symmetry-induced underestimation arises from late grouping processes, such as those involved in incremental grouping, supporting object segmentation.

papers.title: Interrater agreement of seizure onset and spread in scalp EEG
papers.abstract: Objective. Faster seizure spread on intracranial EEG has been linked to worse surgical outcome. If contralateral spread on scalp EEG carried similar prognostic information, it could identify poor resection candidates before intracranial monitoring and direct them toward neuromodulation sooner. Testing this first requires that experts reliably annotate spread on scalp EEG. The interrater agreement for seizure spread detection on scalp EEG is unknown; prior scalp EEG reliability studies have focused mainly on seizure detection. We quantified expert agreement on the laterality, channels, and timing of seizure onset and contralateral spread. Methods. We retrospectively analyzed 79 seizures from 48 patients undergoing presurgical evaluation at a single center. Three board certified epileptologists independently marked the time and channels of onset and contralateral spread for each seizure. We measured agreement on onset laterality and spread presence with Gwet k, channels with Cohen k, and timing with the median absolute deviation (MAD). Interrater and majority vote consensus agreement were estimated with patient-clustered CIs. Results. Onset laterality showed substantial interrater agreement (Gwet k = 0.73, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.83); most disagreement involved bilateral onsets. Contralateral spread agreement was comparable (0.63, 0.48 to 0.76). Channel level agreement was higher for onset (inter rater Cohen k = 0.57) than for spread (0.38). Onset timing was highly consistent (median MAD 0.40 s); spread timing agreement was also high (1.99 s), but less so than onset timing (sign rank p < 0.001). Agreement did not differ across annotators or between temporal and non-temporal epilepsy. Significance. Epileptologists generally agree on onset laterality and whether and when seizures spread contralaterally, although spread channels are identified less reliably. These findings support the feasibility of measuring scalp EEG spread as a candidate noninvasive marker of seizure network extent. The public annotated dataset provides a multi-expert reference standard for developing automated spread detection algorithms.

papers.title: Association of the 2HELPS2B Score With Impaired Recovery of Consciousness and In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
papers.abstract: Persistent impairment of consciousness after sedation withdrawal represents a diagnostic and prognostic challenge in critically ill patients, particularly in the absence of major structural brain injury. The 2HELPS2B score is an established electroencephalographic tool for seizure-risk stratification; however, its association with neurological improvement and mortality remains insufficiently investigated. We conducted an exploratory multicenter retrospective observational study, including 33 critically ill adults with persistent impairment of consciousness, defined as a Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR) score <7 persisting for more than 72 hours after sedation withdrawal. Patients with major structural brain injury, severe metabolic abnormalities, or incomplete clinical or electroencephalographic records were excluded. All patients underwent clinically indicated 40-minute video-electroencephalography between the fourth and fifth day after sedation withdrawal. Patients were categorized according to their 2HELPS2B score (≥2 versus <2). The primary outcome was failure to demonstrate any increase in FOUR score during ICU follow-up, and the secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Crude risk ratios (RRs) were calculated, and comparisons were performed using two-sided Fisher's exact tests. Nine (27.3%) patients had a 2HELPS2B score ≥2. Failure to improve FOUR score occurred in four of nine (44.4%) patients with scores ≥2 compared with one of 24 (4.2%) patients with scores <2 (crude RR: 10.67; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.37-83.11; Fisher's exact p=0.013). In-hospital mortality occurred in five of nine (55.6%) patients versus five of 24 (20.8%) patients, respectively (crude RR: 2.67; 95% CI: 1.01-7.07; Fisher's exact p=0.090). CIs were calculated using the approximate logarithmic method. Both estimates were unadjusted and based on a limited number of events. In this small, selected retrospective cohort, a 2HELPS2B score ≥2 was associated with failure to demonstrate improvement in FOUR score during ICU follow-up. Although mortality was numerically higher in the high-score group, the difference was not statistically significant using Fisher's exact test. These preliminary findings do not establish independent prognostic utility or incremental value beyond clinical assessment. Larger prospective studies are required to validate these exploratory associations.

papers.title: An investigation into the cognitive influences on caloric-induced cortical alpha suppression and vestibular responsiveness.
papers.abstract: This study examined the relative contributions of cognitive tasking on cortical alpha suppression during the caloric test and assessed its relationship to peak slow‑phase velocity (pSPV). Electroencephalography (EEG) and electronystagmography (ENG) were performed across three experimental conditions: active (real) and sham caloric testing with and without tasking. Suppression of the alpha rhythm (8-13 Hz) was defined as a global reduction in amplitude relative to baseline. The degree of nystagmus was derived from the pSPV measured during the caloric response. EEG and ENG recordings were obtained from 20 healthy adults with no otologic or neurologic history (mean age = 25.1 ± 3.1 years). Tasking (mental arithmetic) resulted in the largest global reduction in cortical alpha suppression, reflecting changes in both periodic and aperiodic components, when compared to no-tasking conditions (p < 0.001), and a group-level increase in pSPV (p = 0.033). Individual changes in periodic alpha features and the aperiodic exponent were not associated with changes in pSPV (p > 0.05). Caloric-induced cortical alpha suppression was mainly influenced by cognitive state rather than peripheral vestibular drive alone. While the effect of tasking on pSPV is well known, the absence of an association between task-related EEG changes in periodic/aperiodic activity and pSPV suggests that cortical activity and vestibulo-ocular reflex output may be influenced by independent mechanisms.

papers.title: Shared Neural Dynamics of Sentence-Level Language Processing in Verbally Proficient Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: Autistic individuals often show atypical language development during childhood, yet many attain typical language proficiency by adulthood. This raises the question of whether the neural processes supporting language differ in autism once language has been acquired. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we compared verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults during rapid serial visual presentation of structured sentences and pseudoword lists. Sentence processing elicited oscillatory responses across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands, with distinct spatiotemporal profiles and hemispheric lateralization most pronounced in the theta, alpha, and beta bands. Notably, beta-band activity increased over sentence position and was positively associated with verbal ability, consistent with a role in the maintenance and integration of linguistic information. These effects were highly comparable across groups, with similar patterns observed at both the individual and group levels and across sensor- and source-level analyses. Together, these findings indicate largely shared neural dynamics of sentence-level language processing in verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults, suggesting that atypical language-related neural organization is not an inevitable feature of autism in adulthood.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in epilepsy care: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical applications in diagnosis, classification, outcome prediction, and surgical decision-making.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, with disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries where access to specialized care remains limited. Despite advances in neuroimaging and electrophysiology, accurate diagnosis, etiological classification, and timely identification of surgical candidates remain major clinical challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to integrate multimodal data and support clinical decision-making across the epilepsy care continuum. To systematically assess and meta-analytically quantify the evidence on AI applications for diagnosis, etiological classification, outcome prediction, surgical candidate selection, and workflow optimization in epilepsy. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251117939). Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Cochrane Library, and SciELO for studies published between January 2014 and March 2026. Eligible studies included original research in human subjects with epilepsy applying AI or machine learning models and reporting at least one quantitative performance metric with internal or external validation. Study quality was assessed using PROBAST. Pooled estimates of Area Under the Curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity were derived using DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models across four clinical task groups: diagnosis, classification, outcome prediction, and surgical referral. From 423 identified records, 102 studies met inclusion criteria. Research output increased markedly after 2018, peaking in 2021 and 2024, with geographic concentration in China (n = 31) and the United States (n = 11). Electroencephalography and MRI were the dominant input modalities, and Support Vector Machines (n = 41) and Convolutional Neural Networks (n = 22) were the most frequently employed algorithms. Most studies relied exclusively on internal validation, and external validation remained scarce across all domains. PROBAST assessment revealed high risk of bias in the majority of studies, particularly in the participant and analysis domains. Meta-analysis demonstrated strong discriminative performance across all groups: the classification group achieved the highest pooled AUC (0.929; 95% CI: 0.837-0.971), followed by diagnosis (0.899; 95% CI: 0.859-0.929), surgical referral (0.895; 95% CI: 0.870-0.916), and outcome prediction (0.807; 95% CI: 0.740-0.861). Sensitivity was highest in the diagnosis group (0.885; 95% CI: 0.840-0.918) and lowest in surgical referral (0.729; 95% CI: 0.681-0.771), a clinically relevant asymmetry given the high cost of missing true surgical candidates in drug-resistant epilepsy. Substantial variability was observed across studies, reflecting differences in data modalities, AI architectures, and sample sizes, and indicating that pooled estimates should be interpreted with caution rather than as fixed, generalizable performance figures. AI demonstrates robust and clinically meaningful performance across the spectrum of epilepsy care, particularly for diagnosis and surgical planning. However, uniformly high between-study heterogeneity, predominant reliance on internal validation, variable study quality, and underrepresentation of low- and middle-income country contexts limit the generalizability of current evidence and hinder clinical translation. Prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, and context-adapted implementation strategies are essential to realize the full clinical potential that this body of evidence consistently demonstrates.

papers.title: Direct cortical electrical stimulation-induced seizures: Are they reliable? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: We aimed to assess the frequency, clinical relevance, and prognostic value of stimulation-induced seizures (SIS) during intracranial EEG recording (iEEG), and to compare high-frequency (HF) and low-frequency (LF) stimulation protocols. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies reporting SIS during preoperative iEEG. Pooled proportions of SIS and habitual seizures were estimated using random-effects models. Differences between HF and LF stimulation were assessed using odds ratios. Study-level meta-regression was conducted to evaluate associations between SIS rates, habitual seizure proportions, and postoperative favorable seizure outcome (Engel Ia). Twenty-five studies were included. SIS occurred more frequently with HF than LF stimulation (56.1% vs. 35.8%; OR 1.83, 95% CI 1.50-2.23; p < 0.001), with substantial between-study heterogeneity. Among patients with SIS, LF stimulation was associated with a higher proportion of habitual seizures compared to HF (81.8% vs. 72.9%), although this difference was not statistically significant. A higher proportion of habitual electro-clinical seizures among SIS correlated with increased rates of favorable seizure outcomes with LF stimulation (p = 0.004) but not with HF stimulation (p = 0,912). Finally, MRI-visible lesions and the mesio-temporal seizure-onset zone were associated with higher SIS rates (p < 0.01). In conclusion, HF stimulation increases the likelihood of inducing SIS, but SIS frequency was not associated with a higher proportion of favorable seizure outcomes. Instead, the clinical relevance of SIS depends on their similarity to habitual seizures. These findings suggest that SIS may reflect underlying network excitability, and that their diagnostic value lies in their semiological and EEG concordance rather than occurrence of stimulated seizures alone. Overall, these results emphasize the importance of stimulation-induced habitual electro-clinical seizures for postsurgical outcome prognostication.

papers.title: Label-Free Live Cell Type Prediction by Integrating Raman Spectroscopy and Machine Learning.
papers.abstract: Coherent Raman spectroscopy enables label-free biochemical fingerprinting of live cells with subcellular resolution. We previously developed a machine learning framework capable of classifying glioma FFPE tissues using Raman spectral signatures. To accelerate live cell acquisition, we previously developed RADAR (Raman Spectral Analysis Using Deep Learning for Artifact Removal), a method that increases imaging speed by an order of magnitude while preserving spectral integrity. By integrating high-speed Raman imaging with supervised machine learning, we aimed to define unique biochemical fingerprints specific to cell type. We hypothesized that intrinsic biochemical composition alone is sufficient to distinguish cellular identity and tumor subtype. To test this, we generated metabolic maps of diverse brain-derived cell types-including astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, and glioblastoma cells-using coherent Raman spectroscopy at single-cell resolution. Patient-derived brain tumor cell lines representing genetically heterogeneous backgrounds were analyzed. Samples were stratified by IDH1 mutation status (IDH1-mutant and IDH1-wild-type) and histologically classified as oligodendroglioma or astrocytoma. Raman spectral data were acquired from 286 live single cells across the two principal molecular classes, with further subdivision into two histologic subtypes within the IDH1-mutant group. Classification was performed using an XGBoost model with shallow tree depth (1-3), a 20% held-out test set, and grouped, stratified 5-fold cross-validation to control for sample-level bias. The machine learning framework distinguished IDH1-mutant from IDH1-wild-type cells with a ROC-AUC of 0.78 and further discriminated IDH1-mutant astrocytoma from oligodendroglioma cells with a ROC-AUC of 0.81. Feature importance analysis demonstrated that separation between IDH1-mutant and IDH1-wild-type cells was driven primarily by Raman peaks associated with protein amide bands, total NADH, unsaturated fatty acids, and heme-related vibrational modes. Within the IDH1-mutant class, discrimination between oligodendroglioma and astrocytoma was driven by lipid-rich vesicle signatures, protein/polyamide amide bands, and lipid-associated spectral features. Together, these findings support the feasibility of label-free, machine learning-assisted Raman profiling to resolve clinically relevant glioma subtypes at single-cell resolution. This scalable analytical framework provides a translational platform for investigating metabolic heterogeneity, therapeutic response, co-culture systems, and patient-derived organoid models.

papers.title: Multifunctional CNT-based Platform for Enhanced Dopaminergic Differentiation and Electrochemical Dopamine Sensing from Human iPSC-derived Neurons.
papers.abstract: Pairing neuro-electrochemical sensors with physiologically relevant neuronal models represents a new frontier in the study of neurodegenerative diseases. In this work, we reported an electroactive platform for in situ detection of dopamine, combining human iPSC-derived neurons with carbon nanotubes. In this system, carbon nanotubes served a triple role: enhancing the electroactive area, catalyzing dopamine oxidation, and promoting subtype-specific dopaminergic differentiation. We developed a robust protocol achieving functional dopaminergic neurons, confirmed via qPCR, immunocytochemistry, MEA electrophysiology, and calcium imaging. CNT substrates were associated with a significant increase in the TH/neurofilament overlap (37.90 {+/-} 3.80% vs. 26.01 {+/-} 3.75% in controls). Applying differential pulse voltammetry and chronoamperometry, we quantified extracellular dopamine at 1.25 M and confirmed the stimulus-dependent release induced by benztropine and KCl depolarization. Post-electrochemical immunostaining confirmed that neurons retained their morphology and TH expression. Overall, this work establishes a novel framework for neurodegenerative disease modeling that recapitulates key electrophysiological and neurochemical features of dopaminergic neurons, representing a powerful tool for disease modeling, drug screening, and the development of next-generation neuro-biosensors.

papers.title: Seizure Freedom After Focal Epilepsy Surgery in a Child With Tuberous Sclerosis Complex and Coexisting Suspected Subependymal Giant Cell Astrocytoma: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: We report a three-year-old girl with tuberous sclerosis complex and drug-resistant focal epilepsy who achieved clinical seizure freedom after left frontal resection. Seizures began at three months of age and continued despite multiple antiseizure medications, occurring approximately 11-16 times daily. Medical records reported a TSC1 mutation, although the original genetic report was unavailable. Preoperative examination documented developmental delay, absence of spoken language and independent walking, and right-sided hemiparesis graded 4/5. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multiple cortical and subcortical lesions, a prominent left frontal abnormality, and a separate right lateral ventricular lesion considered radiologically suggestive of a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma. Presurgical video-electroencephalography recorded multiple focal motor seizures and subclinical seizure patterns associated with left frontal activity at F3-C3, together with interictal discharges in the same region. Following multidisciplinary assessment, microsurgical resection was performed using neuronavigation, intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, and bipolar stimulation before resection. Intraoperative electrocorticography was not performed. The subsequent neurosurgical record reported the histological diagnosis of the resected frontal specimen as giant cell astrocytoma, grade I; the original pathology report and slides were unavailable for independent review. The separate ventricular lesion remained unresected. At 18-month follow-up, no clinical seizures had been reported since surgery while antiseizure treatment continued. Independent walking and syllabic speech had emerged, although developmental impairment remained. Right-sided hemiparesis was graded 4/5 both before surgery and at follow-up; the intervening postoperative motor course was incompletely documented. Follow-up electroencephalography demonstrated epileptiform activity despite clinical seizure freedom. This case illustrates a favorable seizure outcome after localized surgery in a child with multiple intracranial lesions, while emphasizing the distinction between clinical seizure control, electroencephalographic findings, and reported pathological diagnoses.

papers.title: EEG and fNIRS evidence for brain responses to three tannins: implications for astringency surface sub-quality in red wine.
papers.abstract: The astringency surface sub-quality is pivotal to red wine perception, yet its neural bases remain unclear. The approaches of non-invasive neurophysiological techniques, sensory analysis, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis, and molecular docking were applied to examine the astringency surface sub-quality responses to three tannins-tannic acid, grape tannin and wine tannin-standardized to equivalent astringency intensity. The results showed that the three tannins at iso-intensity evoked distinct brain activity and sensory responses (wine tannin > tannic acid > grape tannin). The electroencephalography (EEG) results showed that frontal activation was significantly higher than in other regions, with differential delta-band power, while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) revealed corresponding changes in oxygenated hemoglobin across different frontal cortical regions, most prominently at channel 6 in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. LC-MS analysis of tannins indicated that higher levels of tannin oligomers, polymeric pigments and free anthocyanins were associated with finer astringency sub-quality and stronger neurophysiological responses. By establishing a clear link between chemical composition and neural activation, this investigation demonstrates the efficacy of using neurophysiological measures as a robust, objective tool to complement and refine traditional sensory evaluation of wine.

papers.title: Intranasal embelin-nanostructured lipid carrier with β-cyclodextrin inclusion complex (EBCD) produces sustained behavioural control of convulsive activity in the lithium-pilocarpine rat model: A behavioural and neurochemical comparison with intranasal diazepam.
papers.abstract: Status epilepticus (SE) is a neurological emergency requiring rapid behavioural control of convulsive activity. First-line benzodiazepines are frequently administered through delayed or invasive routes, and lose effectiveness as seizure persist. This study evaluated an intranasal embelin-β-cyclodextrin nanostructured lipid carrier (EBCD) as a behavioural proof-of-concept treatment in the lithium-pilocarpine rat model, using intranasal diazepam as reference. papers.title: Machine learning-assisted fusion of urinary Raman and fluorescence spectra for detection of urothelial carcinoma.

In contrast, an artificial neural network (ANN) applied to full spectral data significantly improved classification performance, reaching accuracies above 90% when combined with data augmentation. These results demonstrate that the multimodal spectroscopy approach, particularly when coupled with advanced machine learning strategies, can enable effective non-invasive detection of UC. Despite limitations related to fibre-probe measurements and bulk urine variability, the proposed approach represents a promising step toward rapid and cost-effective bladder cancer screening.

papers.title: A synaptic mitochondrion-ribbon-vesicle complex organizes photoreceptor neurotransmission.

papers.title: Membrane Lipid Composition and Asymmetry Modulate Translocation Versus Leakage of the Model Amphipathic Peptide MAP.
papers.abstract: Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) can enable intracellular access while avoiding cytotoxicity, yet their behavior is highly sensitive to membrane composition. Polarized ATR-FTIR provides structural context, indicating predominantly membrane-associated α-helical conformations across lipid compositions. Together, these results establish lipid asymmetry and composition as actionable biointerface parameters that tune CPP function between translocation and leakage and demonstrate an experimentally benchmarked framework for predicting membrane outcomes across complex lipid environments.

papers.title: JAK Inhibition in Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome: A Case Series from Sydney Children's Hospital.

Pathogenesis appears to involve innate immune dysregulation, and first-line immunotherapy (intravenous immunoglobulin [IVIG], corticosteroids) is ineffective in most cases. A number of second-line cytokine-directed therapies have been trialled in individual case reports and short case series, but with similarly unencouraging outcomes.
